name: Set Maat (Deir el-Medina)
other_names: Pa-demi; workmen's village at Deir el-Medina, Luxor West Bank, Egypt
making_significance: The village housed the crews who cut and painted the royal tombs in the Valley of the Kings, and its ostraca record wages, tools, named craftsmen and a strike.
leaves_out: women and household labour; water-carriers and support staff living outside the village
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);British Museum collection search (link-out);Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports
notes: links: MKR090; CIV001. The strike under Ramesses III is recorded in the Turin Strike Papyrus.

name: Akhetaten workshops
date_note: approx.; reign of Akhenaten and shortly after
making_significance: Excavated workshops at Akhenaten's short-lived capital, including the compound attributed to the sculptor Thutmose where the Nefertiti bust was found in 1912, show how royal sculpture, glass and faience were made.
object_types: site type: sculptors' workshops and craft quarter;bust;plaster cast;faience ring;glass vessel
leaves_out: apprentices and unnamed workers in the compound
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports;British Museum collection search (link-out)
notes: Attribution to Thutmose rests on an inscribed ivory horse blinker. Egypt has requested return of the Nefertiti bust from Berlin.

name: Fustat
date_note: approx.; founded 641-42; burned 1168; pottery production continued after
making_significance: Fustat's workshops and rubbish mounds yielded lustreware, local copies of Chinese ceramics and imported sherds that document how potters copied and traded across the Indian Ocean.
object_types: site type: city and pottery centre;lustreware;sgraffito ware;Chinese export sherd;textile fragment
defined_by: archaeologists (Aly Bahgat; George Scanlon for ARCE)
leaves_out: the Geniza merchant community; potters known only by signatures
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports;British Museum collection search (link-out)
notes: links: MKR013; DIA004. The Cairo Geniza was kept in the Ben Ezra Synagogue at Fustat.

name: Wadi Hammamat quarries
making_significance: Rock inscriptions record expeditions that quarried greywacke (bekhen stone) for royal statues and vessels, and the Turin Papyrus Map depicts the area.
object_types: site type: quarry and expedition route;statue;rock inscription;vessel
leaves_out: expedition labourers named only as numbers in inscriptions
notes: Turin Papyrus Map dated c. 1150 BCE.

name: Aswan granite quarries
making_significance: The northern quarry with its unfinished obelisk shows how workers extracted granite with dolerite pounders for obelisks, statues and sarcophagi.
leaves_out: quarry workers
notes: Date of the unfinished obelisk (often given as New Kingdom) to verify.

name: Serabit el-Khadim
date_note: approx.; Middle and New Kingdom expeditions
making_significance: Turquoise-mining expeditions left a temple to Hathor and Proto-Sinaitic inscriptions that are among the earliest known alphabetic writing.
object_types: site type: mine and temple;turquoise;Proto-Sinaitic inscription;stela
functions: clothing and adornment;record and writing;ritual and belief
leaves_out: the Canaanite and Sinai workers whose script it probably is
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;British Museum collection search (link-out);open-access excavation reports

name: Wadi Allaqi
date_note: approx.; pharaonic to medieval Islamic mining
making_significance: Gold mines along Wadi Allaqi supplied Egyptian states and, later, medieval Islamic mints, with mining camps described by Arab geographers.
object_types: site type: gold-mining district;grinding stone;ore mill
leaves_out: miners, including convicts and war captives described in ancient accounts of Eastern Desert gold mines
notes: Agatharchides (via Diodorus) describes coerced labour in Ptolemaic gold mines; whether he meant Allaqi is uncertain.

name: Mons Porphyrites
other_names: Gebel Abu Dukhan, Eastern Desert, Egypt
making_significance: These imperial quarries were the source of the purple porphyry used for Roman and Byzantine imperial statues, columns and sarcophagi.
leaves_out: quarry workers; Christians condemned to the 'Porphyry quarry in Thebais' in the persecution of the early 4th c.
notes: Condemned labour attested by Eusebius, Martyrs of Palestine 8.1; its scale beside the regular workforce is unknown.

name: Berenike
other_names: Berenike Troglodytica, Red Sea coast, Egypt
making_significance: The Red Sea port traded with India, Arabia and East Africa, and excavations found Indian teak, pepper, beads, textiles and ostraca.

name: Qantir-Piramesse
making_significance: Crucibles and furnaces excavated at Qantir show that glass was made here from raw materials, beside large bronze-casting workshops.
object_types: site type: royal city and workshop area;glass ingot;crucible;chariot fitting
notes: links: INV026. Rehren and Pusch, Science 2005.

name: Egyptian Museum (Tahrir)
other_names: Museum of Egyptian Antiquities, Cairo, Egypt
date_note: building opened 1902; collection begun at Bulaq 1858
making_significance: The museum was the centre of the French-led Antiquities Service, whose partage rules decided which finds stayed in Egypt and which went abroad.
defined_by: the Egyptian state; Antiquities Service (Mariette; Maspero)
leaves_out: Egyptian excavators and workers; finds exported under partage
notes: Objects were stolen during the 2011 break-in; some recovered.

name: Grand Egyptian Museum
making_significance: The museum near the Giza pyramids brings together Tutankhamun's full tomb group and conservation laboratories, and is part of Egypt's case for the return of objects held abroad.
object_types: site type: museum and conservation centre;tomb group;statue

name: Kerma
making_significance: The capital of Kerma had workshops for faience, bronze and thin black-topped beakers around the mud-brick temple known as the Western Deffufa.
object_types: site type: capital, workshops and cemetery;beaker;faience inlay;dagger
functions: ritual and belief;rule and display;food and storage
free_sources: collection search link-out only;Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports
notes: links: ARC019; POL002. Reisner finds at MFA Boston (link-out).

name: Meroë
date_note: approx.; royal city from c. 6th c. BCE
making_significance: Slag heaps at Meroë attest large-scale iron smelting, and the royal city had workshops for pottery, faience and gold jewellery beside its pyramid cemeteries.
object_types: site type: royal city, iron-working site and cemetery;pyramid;jewellery;painted pottery
leaves_out: Giuseppe Ferlini's destruction of pyramids in 1834 to take the Amanishakheto treasure
free_sources: open-access excavation reports;Wikimedia Commons;British Museum collection search (link-out)
notes: links: POL003. Ferlini treasure now in Berlin and Munich.

name: Jebel Barkal
making_significance: The sacred mountain of Amun had temples and royal cemeteries whose stone and bronze commissions record Kushite kingship.
object_types: site type: sacred mountain, temples and cemetery;statue;stela
free_sources: open-access excavation reports;Wikimedia Commons;collection search link-out only

name: Qasr Ibrim
making_significance: The dry citadel preserved textiles, leather, basketry and manuscripts in Meroitic, Old Nubian, Coptic, Greek and Arabic across about three thousand years.
free_sources: open-access excavation reports;British Museum collection search (link-out)
notes: Now an island in Lake Nasser.

name: Faras Cathedral
other_names: Pachoras; Lower Nubia (now under Lake Nasser)
date_note: approx.; cathedral rebuilt c. 707, painted in phases to 12th c.
making_significance: Wall paintings rescued in 1961-64 before flooding document Nubian Christian painting across several centuries.
leaves_out: the split of the paintings between Warsaw and Khartoum; displaced Nubian communities
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports;collection search link-out only

name: Old Dongola
making_significance: The capital of Makuria had churches, a throne hall and painted monasteries whose murals and pottery show Nubian Christian workshops.

name: Sudan National Museum
making_significance: The museum holds finds from the Nubian rescue campaign, including temples re-erected in its garden, and was reported looted during the war from 2023.
defined_by: the Sudanese state; UNESCO Nubian campaign
leaves_out: communities displaced by the Aswan High Dam

name: Taforalt
other_names: Grotte des Pigeons, Oriental region, Morocco
date_note: approx.; beads c. 82,000 BP; Iberomaurusian cemetery c. 15,000-13,000 BP
making_significance: Perforated Nassarius shells with ochre, dated to about 82,000 years ago, are among the earliest known beads, and the cave later held an Iberomaurusian cemetery.

name: Carthage
date_note: traditional foundation 814 BCE; Punic city destroyed 146 BCE; Roman city to 698
making_significance: The Punic port with its circular naval harbour, dye works and potters' quarters anchored a Mediterranean trade network, and the later Roman city made mosaics and lamps.
leaves_out: the people buried in the Tophet, whose interpretation is contested
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;Met Open Access (CC0);British Museum collection search (link-out);open-access excavation reports

name: Chemtou
date_note: approx.; quarrying from the later 2nd c. BCE, ceasing after 235 CE
making_significance: Quarries at Simitthus supplied yellow 'giallo antico' marble across the Roman world, with a walled workers' camp and workshops beside them.
object_types: site type: quarry and workshop camp;column;veneer
leaves_out: quarry workers, including prisoners and presumed forced labourers
notes: DAI describes the camp as a labour camp for the imperial administration, prisoners and workmen; the workforce status is inferred, not documented in detail.

name: Kairouan
making_significance: The Great Mosque's mihrab is framed by 9th-century lustre tiles linked to Iraq, and the city later became a carpet-weaving centre.
object_types: site type: city, mosque and craft centre;lustre tile;minbar;carpet
leaves_out: women carpet weavers
notes: Whether all mihrab tiles were imported from Iraq or partly made locally is debated.

name: Chouara tannery
date_note: approx.; tanneries attested for centuries, founding date uncertain; ongoing
making_significance: The dye and tanning pits of the Fez medina process hides into leather by hand, a working district tied to the city's craft guilds.
leaves_out: tannery workers' health and wages
notes: links: MKR014. Founding date to verify.

name: Sijilmasa
making_significance: Sijilmasa was the northern Saharan terminus of the gold trade and minted gold dinars from West African gold.
object_types: site type: caravan city and mint;dinar
leaves_out: enslaved people carried north by the same caravans

name: Mogador
date_note: approx.; Phoenician outpost 7th-6th c. BCE; dye works under Juba II
making_significance: The island was a Phoenician trading post and later a dye works associated with the Gaetulian purple mentioned by Pliny.
object_types: site type: island trading post;amphora;dye works
notes: Link between the island and Juba II's purple dye works to verify.

name: Timbuktu
making_significance: Timbuktu's mosques and family libraries hold manuscripts copied, bound and traded in the city, which was also a market for salt, gold and books.
object_types: site type: trading city and manuscript centre;manuscript;binding;mosque
leaves_out: enslaved and servile workers in the trans-Saharan trade; the 2012 destruction of mausoleums
notes: links: MKR010; POL036; POL037. Manuscripts were evacuated to Bamako in 2012-13.

name: Djenné
date_note: town from c. 13th c.; Great Mosque rebuilt 1907; ongoing
making_significance: The barey masons' corporation leads the yearly replastering of the Great Mosque in mud, a collective building practice in a trading town of the inland Niger Delta.
object_types: site type: town, mosque and masons' quarter;mud-brick building
leaves_out: women and youths who carry water and plaster

name: Djenné-Djeno
making_significance: Excavations found an urban cluster with iron-working, potting and imported glass beads that predates the trans-Saharan caravan trade.
leaves_out: the looting of Inland Niger Delta terracottas for the art market

name: Gao
date_note: approx.; Gao-Saney 7th-10th c.; Songhay capital 15th-16th c.
making_significance: Gao was a Niger River market whose royal cemetery had inscribed marble stelae imported from al-Andalus, and later the capital of Songhay.
object_types: site type: river market and capital;tombstone;bead;tomb
notes: links: POL037. Almería origin of the stelae to verify.

name: Essouk-Tadmekka
making_significance: Excavations found clay coin moulds of about the 11th century, evidence that gold was cast into coin blanks inside the Sahara.

name: Taghaza
making_significance: Ibn Battuta described Taghaza in 1352 as a salt-mining town built of salt blocks, where the salt was cut by enslaved workers.
leaves_out: the enslaved miners

name: Kofar Mata dye pits
date_note: tradition dates the pits to the late 15th c.; ongoing
making_significance: Dyers work indigo in cement-lined pits at Kofar Mata, a surviving part of the dyeing industry that made Kano's cloth known across the Sahel.
notes: links: MKR006 (maker-community node for the same dyers; merge or keep as place). Founding date to verify.

name: Masaga glass quarter
making_significance: Glassmakers of the Masaga quarter make bangles and beads by remelting recycled glass, a craft the guild links to Nupe history.

name: Gorée
date_note: European trading post from 15th c.; memorial site
making_significance: Gorée was a European trading post in the Atlantic trade in enslaved Africans and is now a memorial whose House of Slaves is central to debates about how that trade is presented.
object_types: site type: island trading post and memorial;building
leaves_out: the scale of embarkations from Gorée is debated

name: Museum of Black Civilisations
other_names: Musée des Civilisations noires, Dakar, Senegal
making_significance: The museum, first proposed at the 1966 Dakar festival, presents African and diaspora histories and receives returned objects.
notes: links: INS083; EVT022. Place node for the building; merge with INS083 if preferred.

name: Igun Street
other_names: Igun Eronmwon quarter, Benin City, Nigeria
date_note: approx.; oral history dates the guild to the 13th-14th c.; ongoing
making_significance: Igun Street is the hereditary quarter of the Benin brass-casters' guild, where lost-wax casting for the Oba's court continues.
leaves_out: apprentices; women's work in the households

name: Oba's Palace, Benin City
making_significance: The royal palace commissioned Benin's brass plaques, ivories and altar objects and was sacked by the British punitive expedition in February 1897.
object_types: site type: royal palace and altar complex;plaque;carved tusk;altar

name: National Museum, Benin City
date_note: present building opened 1973; a museum was first set up in 1946
making_significance: The museum holds Benin castings left in Nigeria or bought back and is one of the places where returned objects are discussed.
defined_by: the National Commission for Museums and Monuments
notes: Opened to the public 1973 (Wikipedia; Nigerian Observer 2022); 1946 origin from a single press source.

name: National Museum, Lagos
making_significance: The museum, founded by Kenneth Murray, holds Nok, Ife, Igbo-Ukwu and Benin works and shaped how Nigerian antiquities were catalogued and displayed.
defined_by: the Nigerian Antiquities Service (Kenneth Murray; Bernard Fagg)
leaves_out: the excavators and communities from whom objects came

name: Wunmonije Compound
making_significance: Builders digging in the compound in 1938 found the copper-alloy Ife heads that changed European ideas of African casting.
object_types: site type: find site near the palace;cast head
leaves_out: the export of some heads in 1938-39
notes: links: CIV011; POL027. Some heads left Nigeria via William Bascom; verify.

name: Igbo Olokun
making_significance: Crucible fragments and beads show that high-lime, high-alumina glass was made here from local materials, a primary glass industry in West Africa.

name: Igbo-Ukwu
other_names: Igbo Isaiah, Igbo Richard and Igbo Jonah, Anambra State, Nigeria
making_significance: Leaded-bronze castings with fine lost-wax detail, glass beads and a richly furnished burial were excavated at three compounds.
object_types: site type: excavated compounds and burial;vessel;regalia;bead
free_sources: open-access excavation reports;Wikimedia Commons;collection search link-out only

name: Taruga
making_significance: Taruga's furnaces are among the earliest dated iron-smelting sites in West Africa, in the region whose Nok terracottas are heavily looted.
object_types: site type: iron-smelting site and settlement;furnace;terracotta figure
defined_by: archaeologists (Bernard Fagg; Goethe University Frankfurt Nok project)
leaves_out: the looting of Nok terracottas
free_sources: open-access excavation reports;collection search link-out only

name: Jos Plateau tin fields
making_significance: Colonial tin mining exposed the first known Nok terracottas (1928, and more from 1943), and during the Second World War the colonial state imposed forced labour on the mines.
leaves_out: conscripted mine workers
notes: links: ARC028. Wartime forced labour: Freund, J. African History (labour migration to the tin mines 1903-1945).

name: Bonwire
making_significance: Bonwire's weavers make strip-woven kente on narrow looms, with named patterns once reserved for the Asante court.
leaves_out: women spinners and traders; printed kente copies

name: Kumasi
making_significance: The Asante capital commissioned goldwork, cast brass goldweights and regalia, and was looted by British forces in 1874 and again in 1896-1900.

name: Elmina Castle
other_names: São Jorge da Mina, Elmina, Ghana
making_significance: The castle was a Portuguese and then Dutch trading fort for gold and, increasingly, for enslaved Africans held in its dungeons.
object_types: site type: trading fort and dungeon;manilla;cloth

name: Ouidah
making_significance: Ouidah was a principal port of the Atlantic slave trade from the Bight of Benin and today has a memorial route to the beach.
object_types: site type: port and memorial route;cowrie;cloth

name: Abomey Royal Palaces
making_significance: The Dahomey palaces had appliqué workshops and painted clay reliefs, and French troops took royal objects in 1892, 26 of which were returned in 2021.
object_types: site type: royal palace complex;appliqué hanging;throne;relief

name: Krobo bead-making
making_significance: Krobo bead-makers fire powdered recycled glass in clay moulds to make beads worn at the dipo rite and sold at markets.
object_types: site type: bead workshops and market;glass bead

name: Osun-Osogbo Sacred Grove
date_note: grove old; New Sacred Art from 1950s
making_significance: The grove's shrines were rebuilt from the 1950s by Susanne Wenger and local artists of the New Sacred Art, and it is still the site of the annual Osun festival.
defined_by: Osun devotees; Susanne Wenger and collaborators; UNESCO
leaves_out: the Yoruba artists whose work is credited to Wenger

name: Bunce Island
making_significance: British traders held captives at Bunce Island's fort before shipping them to the Americas, including rice-growing Carolina and Georgia.

name: Mbanza Kongo
making_significance: The Kongo capital commissioned raffia cloth, ivory and brass crucifixes, and its links with Portugal also fed the slave trade.
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;exchange and value
leaves_out: captives sold through the capital

name: Loango Bay
making_significance: Loango was a port for enslaved captives and later a centre where carvers made relief-carved ivory tusks for European buyers.
object_types: site type: port and carvers' workshops;carved tusk
leaves_out: captives shipped from the coast

name: Nsheng
making_significance: The Kuba royal capital was the centre for raffia cut-pile and embroidered cloth, carved cups and the ndop king figures.
object_types: site type: royal capital;raffia cloth;ndop figure;cup
leaves_out: women embroiderers
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;collection search link-out only

name: Foumban
other_names: Bamum Palace and Rue des Artisans, Foumban, Cameroon
making_significance: Under Sultan Njoya the royal workshops at Foumban made beadwork, brass and carvings, and an artisans' street continues the work.
object_types: site type: royal palace and craft street;beaded throne;mask;brass pipe

name: Ishango
making_significance: A notched bone tool found at Ishango in 1950 is one of the best-known early tally-like objects.
notes: links: INV011. Interpretations as counting device are debated.

name: Sanga
making_significance: Kisalian burials at Sanga contained copper cross-ingots, iron and fine pottery, marking a regional copper currency.

name: Union Minière mines of Katanga
making_significance: Colonial copper and cobalt mining in Katanga recruited labour by coercion in its early decades and supplied metals for global industry.
leaves_out: forcibly recruited miners

name: Royal Museum for Central Africa
date_note: museum 1910; 1897 colonial exhibition on the site
making_significance: Built as a museum of the Congo Free State, it displayed Congolese objects and, in 1897, Congolese people, and reopened in 2018 after a redesign.
object_types: site type: museum and former exhibition ground;sculpture;mask
leaves_out: the Congolese people exhibited in 1897, seven of whom died

name: Ingombe Ilede
making_significance: Burials here contained copper ingots, gold, glass beads, cloth and wire-drawing tools, linking the Zambezi to Indian Ocean trade.
object_types: site type: settlement and cemetery;copper ingot;wire bangle;bead

name: Gona
making_significance: Stone tools from Gona, about 2.6 million years old, are among the earliest known Oldowan artefacts.
object_types: site type: open-air archaeological locality;stone core;flake

name: Yeha
date_note: approx.; Great Temple c. 7th c. BCE
making_significance: The Great Temple at Yeha shows ashlar masonry and inscriptions linked to South Arabian building traditions.

name: Aksum
making_significance: Aksum's carved granite stelae, coinage and workshops record a Red Sea kingdom, and one stela taken to Rome in 1937 was returned in 2005.
object_types: site type: royal city and stelae field;stela;coin
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports;British Museum collection search (link-out)

name: Adulis
making_significance: Adulis was Aksum's Red Sea port, named in the Periplus, where ivory, tortoiseshell and imports passed through.
defined_by: archaeologists; the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea

name: Lalibela
date_note: approx.; traditionally reign of King Lalibela, c. late 12th-early 13th c.; ongoing
making_significance: Churches carved down into the rock were cut as whole buildings from the living stone and remain in use.

name: Fasil Ghebbi
making_significance: The Gondar royal enclosure and nearby churches such as Debre Birhan Selassie show court patronage of painting and building.

name: Amba Maqdala
date_note: Emperor Tewodros II's fortress; British assault April 1868
making_significance: British forces took manuscripts, crowns and church objects from Maqdala in 1868, and some are now subject to return requests.
object_types: site type: fortress and looting site;manuscript;crown;tabot

name: Harar Jugol
making_significance: The walled city has quarters of basket weavers, bookbinders and painted Harari houses, and a manuscript tradition.

name: Lomekwi 3
making_significance: Stone cores and flakes about 3.3 million years old were reported in 2015 as the earliest known stone tools.
object_types: site type: open-air archaeological locality;stone core;flake
notes: links: ARC001; INV139. Dating and deliberate knapping are debated.

name: Olduvai Gorge
date_note: approx.; Oldowan c. 2.0 million years; Acheulean from c. 1.7 million years
making_significance: Olduvai's layered deposits gave the Oldowan its name and show stone tools changing over about two million years.
object_types: site type: gorge with archaeological localities;chopper;hand axe;flake
leaves_out: Maasai and Tanzanian field workers

name: Olorgesailie
making_significance: Olorgesailie holds dense Acheulean hand-axe sites and, from about 320,000 years ago, obsidian brought from far away and pigment use.
object_types: site type: basin with archaeological localities;hand axe;obsidian point;pigment

name: Panga ya Saidi
making_significance: The cave holds long sequences of stone tools and beads and the burial of a child about 78,000 years ago.
defined_by: archaeologists (Max Planck; National Museums of Kenya)

name: Shanga
making_significance: Excavations at Shanga traced a Swahili town from timber buildings to coral mosques, with beads, local pottery and imports.

name: Kilwa Kisiwani
making_significance: Kilwa's Great Mosque, Husuni Kubwa palace and coin mint served a Swahili port that controlled gold shipped north from Sofala.
object_types: site type: port and palace;coin;mosque;imported porcelain
leaves_out: enslaved labour in later Kilwa trade
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports;British Museum collection search (link-out)
notes: links: POL009; NET011. 18th-19th c. Kilwa Kivinje slave trade.

name: Gede
making_significance: Gede's coral-stone houses, mosques and palace show the plan of a Swahili town with imported Chinese and Islamic ceramics.

name: Lamu Old Town
making_significance: Lamu's carpenters and carvers make carved doors, furniture and dhows in a town whose houses keep Swahili building methods.
object_types: site type: town and craft quarter;carved door;chair;dhow

name: Fort Jesus
making_significance: The Portuguese fort at Mombasa's harbour changed hands between Portugal and Oman and is a museum of the port's trade finds.
leaves_out: enslaved labour in the port

name: Zanzibar Stone Town
making_significance: Stone Town's carved doors and houses were built on the clove, ivory and slave trades, and its slave market closed in 1873.
object_types: site type: port town and former slave market;carved door;chest
leaves_out: the enslaved people traded and those who worked clove plantations

name: Kasubi Tombs
making_significance: The thatched royal tomb house of the Buganda kings is built and maintained by hereditary clans using reed, barkcloth and thatch.

name: Kibiro
making_significance: Women at Kibiro have made salt by filtering and boiling saline soil for centuries, trading it across the Great Lakes region.

name: Blombos Cave
date_note: approx.; ochre toolkit c. 100,000 years; engravings and beads c. 75,000-73,000 years
making_significance: Blombos has an ochre-processing toolkit from about 100,000 years ago, engraved ochre and shell beads, and a crosshatched drawing on stone.
object_types: site type: cave;engraved ochre;shell bead;abalone container

name: Pinnacle Point
other_names: Mossel Bay, Western Cape, South Africa
making_significance: Caves at Pinnacle Point record ochre use and shellfish gathering about 164,000 years ago and, later, heat-treated stone and small blades.

name: Diepkloof Rock Shelter
making_significance: Hundreds of fragments of engraved ostrich-eggshell water containers, about 60,000 years old, show repeated geometric motifs.
object_types: site type: rock shelter;engraved eggshell container

name: Mapungubwe
making_significance: Burials on Mapungubwe Hill included gold-foil animals, and the town traded ivory and gold for Indian Ocean glass beads.
object_types: site type: hilltop capital and burials;gold rhinoceros;bead
leaves_out: descendant communities whose ancestors were exhumed
notes: links: ARC040; CIV014; POL014. Gold was found by prospectors in 1933.

name: Great Zimbabwe
making_significance: Dry-stone enclosures at Great Zimbabwe housed a trading capital, and its carved soapstone birds were removed by colonial collectors and returned in stages, the last in 2026.
object_types: site type: stone-walled capital;soapstone bird;imported ceramic
leaves_out: the colonial denial that Africans built it
notes: links: ARC041; CIV005; POL015. Birds returned from South Africa 1981, Germany (loan agreed 2000, public 2003) and the last, from Groote Schuur, 15 April 2026. See OCC169.

name: Sofala
making_significance: Sofala was the southern Swahili port for Zimbabwean gold and ivory before a Portuguese fort took it over in 1505.

name: Kimberley Mine
making_significance: Diamond mining at the Big Hole used closed compounds to control African migrant workers, a system copied across South African mining.
leaves_out: African miners in the compounds

name: Witwatersrand goldfields
making_significance: The Rand's deep gold mines relied on migrant labour under contract and compound systems, including Chinese indentured workers in 1904-10.
leaves_out: migrant miners from across southern Africa; Chinese indentured labourers

name: Iziko Slave Lodge
making_significance: The VOC housed the people it enslaved in this building, now a museum on slavery at the Cape.
object_types: site type: slave lodge and museum

name: Game Pass Shelter
date_note: approx.; paintings mostly last few thousand years
making_significance: The shelter's painted eland panel is central to readings of San rock painting as religious imagery.

name: Mahilaka
making_significance: Mahilaka was an early walled trading town in north-west Madagascar that imported glass and ceramics and worked chlorite schist.
object_types: site type: trading town;stone vessel;imported ceramic

name: Iharana
making_significance: Graves at Iharana held imported Chinese celadon and carved chlorite-schist vessels and were heavily dug by collectors.

name: Ambohimanga
making_significance: The royal hill of the Merina kings is a sacred site of wooden houses, tombs and ritual gates.

name: Rova of Antananarivo
making_significance: The Merina royal compound combined Malagasy timber building with palaces designed with European craftsmen, and was badly damaged by fire in 1995.

name: Zafimaniry villages
making_significance: Zafimaniry carpenters build and decorate houses and furniture in hardwood with geometric carving, a knowledge on UNESCO's intangible heritage Representative List (proclaimed 2003, inscribed 2008).

name: Aapravasi Ghat
making_significance: The immigration depot processed indentured labourers, mostly from India, who were brought to work Mauritian sugar estates.

name: Ipiutak site
making_significance: Burials at the Ipiutak site contained openwork ivory carvings and ivory masks and eyes, made without the ground-slate tools common elsewhere in the Arctic.
object_types: site type: village and cemetery;ivory openwork carving;burial mask;harpoon head
leaves_out: the Tikiġaq community whose ancestors were excavated
free_sources: open-access excavation reports;collection search link-out only

name: Nunalleq
making_significance: A Yup'ik sod house village preserved in permafrost has yielded tens of thousands of wooden, grass and ivory objects in a dig run with the village corporation.
object_types: site type: excavated village;mask;bentwood bowl;grass basket;doll
functions: clothing and adornment;ritual and belief;food and storage
defined_by: the Quinhagak community (Qanirtuuq Inc.); University of Aberdeen
notes: Coastal erosion prompted the excavation from 2009; finds kept in a local centre.

name: Kinngait Studios
making_significance: The print studio at Kinngait turned drawings by Inuit artists into stonecut and stencil editions sold through an annual collection.
defined_by: the West Baffin Eskimo Co-operative; James Houston
leaves_out: printers and cutters whose names are less visible than the artists'

name: Savissivik
other_names: Cape York meteorite find sites, Greenland
making_significance: Inughuit cold-hammered iron from the Cape York meteorites into blades until Robert Peary removed the largest pieces to New York in 1894-97.
defined_by: the Inughuit; Robert Peary; American Museum of Natural History
leaves_out: the six Inughuit Peary brought to New York in 1897, four of whom died there

name: Qilakitsoq
making_significance: Naturally mummified women and children buried at Qilakitsoq wore sealskin and bird-skin clothing that shows Inuit sewing and tailoring.

name: Hvalsey Church
making_significance: The stone church of the Norse Eastern Settlement is the best-preserved Norse building in Greenland, last documented at a wedding in 1408.

name: L'Anse aux Meadows
date_note: approx.; wood cut with metal blades dated 1021
making_significance: The Norse camp has evidence of bog-iron smelting, carpentry and ship repair, and wood cut with metal tools dated to 1021.
object_types: site type: Norse camp;iron slag;spindle whorl;rivet
leaves_out: the Indigenous peoples of Newfoundland at the time

name: Ozette
date_note: approx.; houses buried by mudslide c. 1700
making_significance: A mudslide buried Makah houses with their wooden boxes, baskets, whaling gear and looms, excavated with the Makah and kept at their museum.
notes: Makah Cultural and Research Center opened 1979.

name: SGang Gwaay Llnagaay
making_significance: The Haida village's house and mortuary poles are carved cedar monuments, several of which were removed to museums in 1957.
object_types: site type: village and mortuary site;mortuary pole;house frontal pole
leaves_out: the smallpox epidemic that emptied the village

name: U'mista Cultural Centre
other_names: Alert Bay, Cormorant Island, BC, Canada
making_significance: Regalia surrendered after the 1921 potlatch at Village Island were taken under the potlatch ban and were partly returned to this Kwakwaka'wakw centre from 1979.
notes: Objects went to the National Museum of Canada, the Royal Ontario Museum and George Heye.

name: Yuquot
other_names: Friendly Cove, Nootka Sound, BC, Canada
making_significance: Yuquot was a focus of the maritime fur trade after 1778, and its Whalers' Shrine was removed to the American Museum of Natural History in 1904.
object_types: site type: village and trading anchorage;shrine;sea-otter pelt
notes: links: NET043. Shrine acquired by George Hunt for Franz Boas.

name: c̓əsnaʔəm
making_significance: The Musqueam village and burial ground gave the Marpole phase its name, and in 2012 Musqueam protests stopped a development on it.
object_types: site type: village and burial ground;stone bowl;ground-slate knife

name: Museum of Anthropology at UBC
making_significance: The museum's Great Hall displays Northwest Coast poles and has developed co-management and loan practices with First Nations.
defined_by: University of British Columbia; First Nations partners

name: Chaco Canyon
making_significance: Chaco's great houses held turquoise, macaw feathers, shell and cylinder jars with cacao residue brought along regional roads.
object_types: site type: ceremonial and trading centre;cylinder jar;turquoise ornament;great house
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports;Smithsonian Open Access (CC0)

name: Cerrillos Hills turquoise mines
date_note: approx.; ancestral Pueblo, Spanish and later mining
making_significance: Ancestral Pueblo miners dug turquoise at Mount Chalchihuitl, one of several sources that supplied Chaco and later trade.
notes: links: NET039. Isotope studies show Chaco turquoise came from several sources.

name: Paquimé
making_significance: Paquimé had macaw breeding pens, shell and copper stores and polychrome pottery, a hub between the Southwest and Mesoamerica.
object_types: site type: town and exchange hub;macaw pen;polychrome jar;shell ornament

name: Mimbres Valley sites
making_significance: Painted black-on-white bowls were placed over the dead with a hole broken through them, and bulldozer looting destroyed many sites.
object_types: site type: village and burial sites;painted bowl
free_sources: open-access excavation reports;collection search link-out only

name: Hubbell Trading Post
making_significance: John Lorenzo Hubbell's post bought Navajo rugs and silver and urged weavers towards designs such as Ganado Red that sold to outside buyers.
leaves_out: Navajo women weavers credited under the trader's name

name: Acoma Pueblo
making_significance: Potters at Acoma make thin-walled, painted jars from local clay, one of the longest-inhabited places in North America.

name: Sikyátki
making_significance: Excavations here in 1895 showed Sikyátki polychrome to the Hano potter Nampeyo, whose revival style changed Hopi pottery.
leaves_out: the Hopi whose ancestors' graves were dug
free_sources: Smithsonian Open Access (CC0);collection search link-out only

name: Santa Fe Plaza
making_significance: The plaza hosts the Indian Market, whose juried categories and prizes have shaped what Native American makers produce for sale.

name: Pipestone quarries
date_note: approx.; quarrying older than date shown; ongoing
making_significance: Plains peoples quarry the red catlinite used for pipe bowls here, a right reserved to Native Americans at the national monument.
defined_by: the Dakota and other Plains nations; National Park Service

name: Cahokia
making_significance: The largest Mississippian town had copper workshops, flint-clay figure carving and mound building, and Mound 72 held mass burials.
object_types: site type: mound centre;copper plate;figurine;chunkey stone
leaves_out: the people sacrificed in Mound 72

name: Poverty Point
making_significance: Hunter-gatherers built concentric earthen ridges and mounds here and brought stone and copper from hundreds of kilometres away.
object_types: site type: earthwork and exchange centre;clay cooking ball;stone bead

name: Spiro Mounds
making_significance: The Craig Mound's burial chamber held engraved shell, copper and textiles and was dug out for sale by a mining company in 1933-35.
object_types: site type: mound centre;engraved shell cup;copper plate;textile
leaves_out: the Caddo and Wichita descendants
free_sources: collection search link-out only;Smithsonian Open Access (CC0)

name: Hopewell Mound Group
making_significance: Hopewell mounds held objects of mica, copper, Yellowstone obsidian and shark teeth, and were dug in 1891-92 for display at the Chicago fair.
object_types: site type: earthwork and burial mounds;mica hand;copper effigy;obsidian blade

name: Lowell mills
making_significance: Lowell's water-powered cotton mills employed young women from New England farms, who wrote and struck over wages and hours, spinning cotton grown by enslaved people.
object_types: site type: mill town;cotton cloth;boarding house
defined_by: industrialists (Boston Associates); the mill women; historians
leaves_out: the enslaved people who grew the cotton
free_sources: Library of Congress HABS/HAER (public domain);Library of Congress (public-domain items);Wikimedia Commons

name: Highland Park Ford Plant
making_significance: Ford introduced the moving assembly line for the Model T here in 1913, dividing car-making into timed tasks.
leaves_out: the migrant workers who bore the pace of the line
free_sources: Library of Congress (public-domain items);Library of Congress HABS/HAER (public domain);Wikimedia Commons

name: Charleston
making_significance: Charleston was a leading port for enslaved Africans, whose skills in rice growing, Colono pottery and basketry shaped the Lowcountry.
notes: links: ARC201; DIA008. International African American Museum at Gadsden's Wharf (opened 2023).

name: Jackson Park
other_names: World's Columbian Exposition grounds, Chicago, USA
making_significance: The 1893 fair displayed industry in the 'White City' and placed peoples in ranked villages on the Midway Plaisance, a model protested by Ida B. Wells and Frederick Douglass.
defined_by: the fair's organisers; anthropologists (F. W. Putnam)
leaves_out: the Indigenous and non-Western people exhibited
free_sources: Library of Congress (public-domain items);Internet Archive (public-domain books);Wikimedia Commons
notes: links: EVT007. Conditions of the people exhibited on the Midway to verify.

name: Smithsonian Institution, National Mall
making_significance: The Smithsonian's museums on the Mall classified American and world material culture, and its Open Access release put millions of images under CC0.

name: Metropolitan Museum of Art
making_significance: The Met's collections and 2017 Open Access policy make it one of the main free image sources for world making, alongside disputes over looted antiquities.
notes: Several antiquities returned to Italy, Egypt and others after seizures; details to verify.

name: Cranbrook
making_significance: Eliel Saarinen's academy campus trained designers such as Charles and Ray Eames, Florence Knoll and Harry Bertoia.
leaves_out: Loja Saarinen's weaving studio and other women's workshops

name: Lake Eden campus
other_names: Black Mountain College, North Carolina, USA
making_significance: Students built the Studies Building and worked in the weaving and pottery studios at Lake Eden under teachers including Anni and Josef Albers.
leaves_out: students' and staff labour on the farm and buildings

name: Templo Mayor precinct
making_significance: Offerings buried in the Mexica main temple include stone, shell, gold and feather work, found in excavations since 1978.

name: Tlatelolco market
making_significance: Spanish writers described the Tlatelolco market's ordered sections for cloth, feathers, obsidian and cacao, and the Colegio de Santa Cruz later produced the Florentine Codex nearby.
object_types: site type: market;cotton mantle;obsidian blade;cacao bean
defined_by: Hernán Cortés; Bernal Díaz; Sahagún's collaborators
leaves_out: the Nahua scholars and painters of the Florentine Codex

name: Teotihuacan
making_significance: Apartment compounds at Teotihuacan housed obsidian, lapidary and pottery workshops and a neighbourhood of Oaxacan migrants.
object_types: site type: city with craft neighbourhoods;obsidian blade;mask;mural
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports;Met Open Access (CC0)

name: Sierra de las Navajas
making_significance: Mines here produced the green-gold obsidian traded across Mesoamerica from Teotihuacan to Aztec times.

name: San Lorenzo
making_significance: Olmec sculptors carved colossal basalt heads at San Lorenzo from stone hauled from the Tuxtla mountains.

name: La Venta
making_significance: Olmec builders at La Venta buried massive serpentine block offerings and jade figurines and celts.
object_types: site type: ceremonial centre;jade celt;figurine;mosaic pavement

name: Aguateca
making_significance: Elite houses burned and abandoned in haste kept the tools of scribes, carvers and weavers where they worked.
object_types: site type: burned elite houses;paint pot;spindle whorl;shell ornament

name: Joya de Cerén
date_note: approx.; buried by volcanic ash c. 600-660
making_significance: Volcanic ash buried a farming village with its pots, tools, stored food and gardens, showing everyday making outside elite centres.

name: Motagua Valley jadeite sources
making_significance: The only known Mesoamerican jadeite came from the Motagua valley, supplying Olmec and Maya carvers.
object_types: site type: stone source;jade celt;jade ornament
notes: Some sources identified after Hurricane Mitch (1998).

name: Sacred Cenote, Chichén Itzá
making_significance: Offerings of gold, jade, copal and textiles were dredged from the cenote in 1904-10 by Edward Thompson and taken to the Peabody Museum.
defined_by: the Maya; Edward H. Thompson; Peabody Museum
notes: Partial returns to Mexico (dates to verify).

name: Sitio Conte
making_significance: Burials at Sitio Conte held hammered gold plaques, cast pendants and painted pottery excavated by Harvard and Penn in the 1930s-40s.
free_sources: collection search link-out only;open-access excavation reports

name: Diquís stone spheres
making_significance: Settlements in the Diquís delta have precisely shaped granodiorite spheres placed in alignments.
object_types: site type: settlements with stone spheres;stone sphere

name: Teyuna
other_names: Ciudad Perdida, Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, Colombia
making_significance: The terraced Tairona town was found by looters in 1972 and remains sacred to the Kogi, Arhuaco, Wiwa and Kankuamo.
object_types: site type: terraced town;gold ornament;stone path

name: Museo del Oro
other_names: Banco de la República, Bogotá, Colombia
making_significance: The bank's gold museum, begun with the purchase of a Quimbaya poporo, holds large collections of pre-Hispanic metalwork.

name: Lake Guatavita
making_significance: Muisca offerings to the lake behind the El Dorado story led colonial and later companies to try to drain it for gold.

name: San Agustín
making_significance: Hundreds of carved stone statues guard mounds and tombs in the San Agustín region.

name: Portobelo
making_significance: Portobelo held the fairs where Peruvian silver met Spanish fleets and where enslaved Africans were landed and sold.
object_types: site type: fair port and fortifications

name: Caguana
making_significance: Stone-lined ball courts at Caguana carry carved petroglyphs of Taíno figures.

name: La Isabela
making_significance: Columbus's first town had a kiln making lead-glazed pottery and metalworking debris, and Taíno were forced to supply it with food and gold.
leaves_out: the Taíno forced to supply the settlers

name: La Hueca-Sorcé
making_significance: Early ceramic-age lapidaries at Sorcé carved amethyst, carnelian and jadeitite into pendants including condor figures.
object_types: site type: settlement and lapidary workshop;condor pendant;bead
notes: links: ARC197; NET042. Chronology and 'Huecoid' label debated.

name: Port Royal
making_significance: Much of the town sank in 1692, preserving pewterers', potters' and pipe-makers' goods in a port that also traded enslaved Africans.
object_types: site type: submerged port town;pewter plate;clay pipe

name: Newton Plantation burial ground
making_significance: The burial ground of enslaved people at a sugar estate is the most studied in the Caribbean, with beads, pipes and a carnelian necklace.
object_types: site type: burial ground;bead necklace;clay pipe

name: Partagás cigar factory
other_names: Real Fábrica de Tabacos Partagás, Havana, Cuba
making_significance: Cigar rollers in Havana's factories paid lectores to read to them while they worked, a practice begun in the 1860s.
leaves_out: the enslaved labour on tobacco and sugar land
notes: Reading practice started 1865 in another Havana factory.

name: Monte Verde
making_significance: Monte Verde preserved wooden foundations, knotted cordage and stored plants, pushing back the date for people in the Americas.
object_types: site type: open-air camp;cordage;wooden stake;stone tool
notes: Acceptance debated in the 1990s; now widely accepted.

name: Caral
making_significance: Platform mounds and sunken plazas at Caral were built with shicra bags of stones by a society that grew cotton for nets.
object_types: site type: early urban centre;platform mound;flute

name: Huaca Prieta
making_significance: Twined cotton textiles from the mound include fabric dyed with indigo about 6,200 years ago, the earliest known indigo use.

name: Chavín de Huántar
making_significance: Stone galleries at Chavín hold carved slabs and the Lanzón, and its imagery spread on textiles and gold across the Andes.
object_types: site type: temple centre;carved slab;gold crown

name: Huaca Rajada
making_significance: After looters broke into a tomb in 1987, archaeologists excavated the intact burial of the 'Lord of Sipán' with gold and copper ornaments.

name: Chan Chan
making_significance: The adobe capital of Chimor had walled palaces and artisans' quarters of metalworkers and weavers, many of whom the Inca moved to Cuzco.
object_types: site type: capital with artisans' quarters;adobe frieze;textile
notes: links: MKR025; POL060. human-flow for Inca relocation of artisans.

name: Qorikancha
making_significance: The Inca temple's walls were sheathed in gold that was stripped in 1533 for Atahualpa's ransom and melted down.

name: Cerro Rico
date_note: silver found 1545; mita from 1573; ongoing mining
making_significance: Silver from Potosí, mined by Andean men drafted under the mita, fed Spanish coinage and the Manila and Chinese silver trade.
object_types: site type: mine and mint town;peso;ingot
leaves_out: the mitayos and enslaved Africans at the mint; child miners today

name: Huancavelica
making_significance: Mercury from Huancavelica, dug by drafted mitayos who were poisoned by it, was used to refine Potosí silver.
leaves_out: the mitayos

name: Chinchorro sites
making_significance: Chinchorro fishers made the earliest known artificially prepared mummies, rebuilt with sticks, reeds and clay.

name: Chuquicamata
making_significance: One of the largest open-pit copper mines supplies copper for wiring and electronics.
leaves_out: Atacameño communities and water loss

name: Chulucanas
making_significance: Potters in Chulucanas make burnished, smoke-resist decorated ceramics developed from the 1960s with reference to ancient Vicús wares.
notes: Denomination of origin "Cerámica de Chulucanas" granted 26 July 2006; 1960s revival and Vicús reference not independently confirmed.

name: Camutins mounds
making_significance: Marajoara mound builders made polychrome burial urns and pottery with incised and painted designs.
free_sources: open-access excavation reports;collection search link-out only

name: Taperinha
making_significance: Pottery from the Taperinha shell mound is among the earliest known in the Americas.

name: Llanos de Mojos settlements
making_significance: Lidar revealed Casarabe towns with platform mounds and causeways in the Amazon savanna.

name: Cueva de las Manos
making_significance: Stencilled hands and hunting scenes were painted here over thousands of years by Patagonian hunter-gatherers.

name: São Miguel Arcanjo
other_names: São Miguel das Missões, Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil
making_significance: Guaraní carvers, masons and musicians worked in the Jesuit reduction whose church and sculpture survive.
leaves_out: the Guaraní makers credited to the Jesuits

name: La Chorrera
making_significance: Rubber collection by the Peruvian Amazon Company at La Chorrera enslaved and killed Uitoto and other peoples, as documented by Roger Casement.
leaves_out: the Uitoto, Bora, Andoke and others

name: Fordlândia
making_significance: Ford built a company town to grow rubber for tyres here, and the plantation failed through leaf blight and worker unrest.
leaves_out: Brazilian workers

name: Puebla potteries
making_significance: Puebla potters made tin-glazed talavera poblana under guild rules, adapting Spanish methods and Chinese blue-and-white designs.
defined_by: the potters' guild; the Mexican state
leaves_out: Indigenous and African workers in the potteries

name: Acapulco
making_significance: Acapulco was the American terminus of the Manila galleon, where Chinese silk and porcelain arrived for silver and enslaved Asians were landed.
leaves_out: enslaved Asian 'chinos'

name: Veracruz
making_significance: Veracruz was New Spain's Atlantic port for the treasure fleets and for enslaved Africans.

name: Cartagena de Indias
making_significance: Cartagena was a main port for enslaved Africans entering Spanish South America and a fortified node of the fleet system.

name: Salvador da Bahia
making_significance: Salvador was Brazil's colonial capital and a major port for enslaved Africans, whose carpenters and gilders worked on its churches.

name: Ouro Preto
making_significance: Enslaved miners dug the gold of Vila Rica, whose churches carry soapstone and wood carving by Aleijadinho and his workshop.
leaves_out: the enslaved miners and the workshop assistants credited to Aleijadinho

name: Valongo Wharf
other_names: Cais do Valongo, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil
making_significance: The stone wharf where hundreds of thousands of enslaved Africans landed was uncovered in 2011 with beads, amulets and pipes.
notes: UNESCO World Heritage 2017 (Valongo Wharf Archaeological Site), verified.

name: Taxco
date_note: silver mining from 1530s; design workshops from 1931
making_significance: William Spratling's workshop from 1931 trained local silversmiths, making Taxco a centre of modern Mexican silver design.
object_types: site type: mining town and workshops;silver jewellery
leaves_out: the Mexican silversmiths who ran the benches

name: Museo Nacional de Antropología
making_significance: The museum's design placed the Mexica hall at its centre, and the moving of a Tlaloc monolith from Coatlinchan for it met local protest.
defined_by: the Mexican state; Pedro Ramírez Vázquez
leaves_out: the Coatlinchan community

name: Xianrendong
date_note: approx.; earliest sherds c. 20,000-19,000 cal BP
making_significance: Potsherds from Xianrendong, dated to about 20,000 years ago, are among the earliest known pottery anywhere, made by hunter-gatherers.

name: Liangzhu
making_significance: Elite graves at Liangzhu held jade cong, bi and axes carved with a repeated face motif, in a walled city with large water-control dams.
object_types: site type: walled city and cemeteries;jade cong;jade bi
free_sources: open-access excavation reports;Wikimedia Commons;Met Open Access (CC0)

name: Yinxu
making_significance: Foundry sites at the late Shang capital produced piece-mould bronze vessels, and the tomb of Fu Hao held hundreds of bronzes and jades.
object_types: site type: royal capital, foundries and tombs;ritual bronze vessel;oracle bone;jade
functions: ritual and belief;record and writing;rule and display
leaves_out: the foundry workers and captives buried in royal tombs
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports

name: Mausoleum of the First Qin Emperor
making_significance: Terracotta figures for the emperor's tomb were made in standardised parts by workshops whose foremen stamped their names, with convict labourers buried nearby.
materials_techniques: modular clay figures;mould and hand building;bronze casting
object_types: site type: imperial tomb complex;terracotta figure;bronze chariot;weapon
leaves_out: the conscript and convict labourers

name: Mogao Caves
date_note: approx.; Library Cave sealed early 11th c.; opened 1900
making_significance: Painted cave temples and the sealed Library Cave, whose manuscripts and the dated 868 Diamond Sutra were taken by Stein, Pelliot and others after 1907, record Silk Road making and faith.
object_types: site type: cave-temple complex and manuscript cache;mural;manuscript;printed scroll;banner
defined_by: Buddhist patrons; archaeologists and explorers; the Dunhuang Academy
leaves_out: the monks and local community who kept the cave; the collectors' dispersal of its contents
free_sources: International Dunhuang Programme (link-out);British Museum collection search (link-out);Wikimedia Commons

name: Chang'an
making_significance: The Tang capital's East and West Markets were regulated trading quarters where Sogdian and other foreign merchants sold goods from across Asia.
object_types: site type: capital with regulated markets;silver vessel;sancai figure

name: Quanzhou
making_significance: Quanzhou was a major Song-Yuan port with a multi-faith merchant community and kilns producing wares for export.
notes: A 13th-c. ship excavated at Houzhu in 1974.

name: Guangzhou
making_significance: Canton was China's southern port for foreign trade, and under the Canton System (1757-1842) its workshops painted export porcelain, enamels and pictures to order.
object_types: site type: port and export workshops;export porcelain;painted enamel;export painting
leaves_out: the painters and decorators who worked to foreign order

name: Jingdezhen
date_note: name from 1004; imperial kiln from 1369; ongoing
making_significance: Jingdezhen's kilns and imperial factory made porcelain in a divided production line, and its blue-and-white travelled worldwide.
object_types: site type: kiln town and imperial factory;blue-and-white jar;dish;vase
functions: food and storage;exchange and value;rule and display
leaves_out: the many named stages of workers behind each piece
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);National Palace Museum Open Data (licence to verify);Wikimedia Commons

name: Longquan kilns
making_significance: Longquan kilns made thick-glazed green celadon traded from Japan to East Africa.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: Ding kilns
making_significance: Ding potters made thin white porcelain fired upside down, whose unglazed rims were then bound in metal.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: Yaozhou kilns
making_significance: Yaozhou kilns made carved and moulded olive-green celadon, especially in the Northern Song.
object_types: site type: kiln complex;carved celadon bowl
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: Yuanmingyuan
date_note: built from 1709; looted and burned October 1860
making_significance: British and French troops looted and burned the imperial garden palaces in 1860, dispersing their porcelain, bronzes and jades to Europe.
object_types: site type: imperial palace-garden and looting site;bronze zodiac head;porcelain;jade

name: Dafen Oil Painting Village
making_significance: Painters in Dafen produce hand-painted copies of famous paintings in large numbers for export and decor markets.
leaves_out: the painters whose skill is sold as reproduction

name: Gangjin celadon kilns
making_significance: Gangjin kilns made Goryeo celadon, including inlaid (sanggam) wares and tiles for the court.
object_types: site type: kiln complex;inlaid celadon vase;tile
free_sources: National Museum of Korea e-museum (KOGL Type 1);Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0)

name: Haeinsa Janggyeong Panjeon
making_significance: More than 80,000 woodblocks of the Tripitaka Koreana are stored in ventilated halls built to keep them from decay.
object_types: site type: temple and woodblock repository;printing block
defined_by: the Goryeo state; the temple; UNESCO
leaves_out: the carvers
free_sources: National Museum of Korea e-museum (KOGL Type 1);Wikimedia Commons

name: Heungdeoksa
making_significance: The Buddhist text Jikji was printed at Heungdeoksa in 1377 with movable metal type, and the only surviving copy is in the Bibliothèque nationale de France.
object_types: site type: temple site and printing museum;printed book
free_sources: National Museum of Korea e-museum (KOGL Type 1);Gallica (public-domain items)

name: Gyeongju
making_significance: Silla royal tombs at Gyeongju held gold crowns, glass vessels from the west and ornaments made in local workshops.
object_types: site type: royal capital and tombs;gold crown;glass vessel
free_sources: National Museum of Korea e-museum (KOGL Type 1);Wikimedia Commons

name: National Museum of Korea
date_note: Yongsan building 2005; origins in 1909 and 1915 museums
making_significance: The national museum's collections trace to palace and colonial museums and are released under open reuse terms.
leaves_out: the colonial-period collecting it inherited
free_sources: National Museum of Korea e-museum (KOGL Type 1)

name: Arita
other_names: Izumiyama and Tengudani kiln sites, Saga, Japan
date_note: porcelain from c. 1616; export via VOC from 1659; ongoing
making_significance: Korean potters brought to Japan after the invasions of the 1590s are credited with finding porcelain stone at Izumiyama, starting Japanese porcelain exported as Imari.
object_types: site type: quarry and kiln town;Imari dish;Kakiemon jar
leaves_out: the Korean potters taken by force
free_sources: ColBase (Japan Government Standard Terms);Rijksmuseum (CC0);Met Open Access (CC0)

name: Seto kilns
making_significance: Seto potters made glazed stoneware from about the 13th century, and 'setomono' became a general word for ceramics.
free_sources: ColBase (Japan Government Standard Terms);Met Open Access (CC0)

name: Bizen kilns
making_significance: Bizen potters fire unglazed stoneware for many days in wood-fired kilns, valued in tea ceremony.
free_sources: ColBase (Japan Government Standard Terms);Met Open Access (CC0)

name: Nishijin
date_note: name from the Ōnin War western camp; ongoing
making_significance: Nishijin weavers make figured silks for kimono and obi and adopted the Jacquard loom after weavers were sent to Lyon in 1872.
leaves_out: family members who do preparatory work
free_sources: ColBase (Japan Government Standard Terms);Met Open Access (CC0)

name: Nagasaki and Dejima
making_significance: Dejima was the only European trading post permitted under Tokugawa rule, shipping Japanese porcelain and lacquer and bringing in books and goods.
object_types: site type: artificial island trading post;export porcelain;lacquer box
leaves_out: Japanese interpreters and workers on the island

name: Tokyo National Museum
making_significance: Japan's oldest museum grew from the 1872 Yushima exhibition and built the national categories of Japanese art.

name: Sannai-Maruyama
making_significance: The Jōmon village used lacquered wares, jade from Itoigawa and obsidian from distant sources, around large post buildings.
object_types: site type: village;lacquered bowl;jade bead;clay figurine
free_sources: open-access excavation reports;ColBase (Japan Government Standard Terms)

name: Shōsōin
making_significance: The imperial storehouse holds objects given in 756 and later, including Tang Chinese, Persian-style and Japanese musical instruments, textiles and glass.
free_sources: collection search link-out only;ColBase (Japan Government Standard Terms)

name: Iwami Ginzan
making_significance: Silver from Iwami, refined by cupellation from the 1530s, fed Japan's trade with China and the Portuguese.
object_types: site type: mine and mining town;silver ingot
leaves_out: the miners

name: Sado Island gold mines
making_significance: Sado's gold and silver mines ran from the Edo period, and Korean workers were mobilised to them during the Second World War.
leaves_out: the Korean labourers and Edo-period forced labour
notes: Framing of Korean labour disputed between states.

name: Tomioka Silk Mill
making_significance: The state silk-reeling mill, set up with a French engineer, trained young women who spread mechanised reeling across Japan.
leaves_out: the women reelers

name: Mehrgarh
making_significance: Mehrgarh records early farming, cotton, drilled teeth and bead-making in South Asia.

name: Harappa
making_significance: Workshops at Harappa made stone beads, shell bangles, faience and seals under standard weights.
object_types: site type: city with craft quarters;carnelian bead;seal;shell bangle
functions: clothing and adornment;record and writing;exchange and value

name: Lothal
making_significance: Lothal had a bead workshop and a large brick basin interpreted as a dock linked to Gulf trade.
object_types: site type: town with dock and workshop;bead;seal

name: Zawar
making_significance: Retorts at Zawar show zinc distilled on an industrial scale by the medieval period, long before Europe.
object_types: site type: mine and smelting site;retort;zinc
notes: links: INV091. Distilled zinc from c. 9th c. CE, commercial scale from c. 12th c.; halted c. 1812 (Kharakwal; Craddock).

name: Arikamedu
making_significance: Arikamedu's finds of Mediterranean amphorae and Arretine ware beside local bead-making show a port in the Roman-Indian trade.

name: Muziris
making_significance: Muziris was the Malabar pepper port named in the Muziris papyrus, probably located at Pattanam.

name: Barygaza
making_significance: The Periplus describes Barygaza as a port exporting cotton cloth, indigo and agate.
defined_by: the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea

name: Calicut
making_significance: Calicut was a pepper and cotton-cloth port under the Zamorins, reached by Vasco da Gama in 1498, and 'calico' is named after it.

name: Chandni Chowk
making_significance: The market street of Shahjahanabad grew with the Mughal karkhanas that made textiles, jewellery and metalwork for court and sale.
object_types: site type: market street and workshops;jewellery;embroidery

name: Varanasi weavers' quarters
other_names: Madanpura and Peeli Kothi, Varanasi, India
making_significance: Weavers in Varanasi, many of them Ansari Muslims, weave Banarasi silk brocades on handlooms.
leaves_out: the weavers' indebtedness to traders

name: Jamdani villages of Rupganj
making_significance: Weavers here make jamdani, a fine cotton with supplementary-weft motifs inserted by hand, successor to Dhaka muslin.
defined_by: the weavers; UNESCO (intangible heritage: "Traditional art of Jamdani weaving", 2013)
leaves_out: women's thread preparation

name: Patan
making_significance: Salvi families in Patan weave double-ikat patola, dyeing warp and weft separately before weaving.

name: Machilipatnam
making_significance: Machilipatnam's dyers and block-printers made the mordant-dyed chintz sought by the Dutch and English companies.
object_types: site type: port and dyeing town;chintz;palampore
defined_by: the dyers; the East India companies

name: Pulicat
making_significance: The VOC's Fort Geldria at Pulicat bought Coromandel chintz and also shipped enslaved people from the coast.
object_types: site type: port and trading fort;chintz
leaves_out: the enslaved people shipped from the Coromandel coast

name: Santiniketan
making_significance: Kala Bhavana under Nandalal Bose taught art alongside local crafts and murals in an open-air setting.
leaves_out: the Santal and craft teachers

name: NID Ahmedabad
making_significance: The design school founded after the Eames India Report of 1958 trained designers to work with Indian craft and industry.
defined_by: the Indian government; the Sarabhai family; Charles and Ray Eames

name: Jokhang and Barkhor
making_significance: The Jokhang temple and the Barkhor pilgrim circuit around it are a centre of Tibetan Buddhist devotion and trade in ritual objects.
object_types: site type: temple and market circuit;statue;thangka
defined_by: Tibetan Buddhists; UNESCO (Jokhang only, added 2000 to the Potala Palace listing)

name: Tabo Monastery
making_significance: Tabo's clay sculptures and wall paintings are among the earliest surviving in western Tibetan Buddhism.
defined_by: the Guge kings; Rinchen Zangpo tradition

name: Patan metal workshops
making_significance: Newar metalworkers cast gilded copper images by lost-wax methods for Nepal and Tibet.

name: Samdzong
making_significance: Cave tombs at Samdzong held a gold-and-silver funerary mask, glass beads and textiles showing trade across the Himalaya.

name: Srinagar
making_significance: Srinagar's workshops wove kani shawls and made papier-mâché and walnut carving for trade.

name: Ban Chiang
making_significance: Burials at Ban Chiang contain bronze and painted pottery, and looting for the market in the 1960s-70s damaged the site.
object_types: site type: settlement and cemetery;painted jar;bronze bangle
free_sources: open-access excavation reports;collection search link-out only

name: Óc Eo
making_significance: The port of Funan had bead and metal workshops and finds from India, China and Rome.

name: Angkor
making_significance: A royal bronze foundry excavated near the Angkor Thom palace shows how Khmer images were cast, beside quarries and kilns that supplied the temples.
object_types: site type: royal capital and foundry;bronze image;stoneware

name: Si Satchanalai kilns
making_significance: Kilns along the Yom river made celadon and painted stoneware exported across Southeast Asia.

name: Bagan
making_significance: Thousands of brick temples at Bagan were painted and decorated, and the town is now a centre of lacquerware.
object_types: site type: temple plain and craft town;mural;lacquer box

name: Hội An
making_significance: Hội An was a trading port where Japanese and Chinese merchants settled and Vietnamese ceramics were shipped.

name: Khao Sam Kaeo
making_significance: Glass and stone bead workshops using South Asian techniques show an early cross-Bay of Bengal craft community.
object_types: site type: port settlement and workshops;bead

name: Leang Tedongnge
making_significance: A painting of a pig dated to at least 45,500 years ago is among the earliest known figurative images.

name: Tabon Caves
making_significance: The Manunggul burial jar's lid shows two figures in a boat, found among long-used burial caves.

name: Manila
making_significance: Manila joined Chinese junks to the galleons for Acapulco, and Chinese craftsmen in the Parián carved ivory saints for the Americas.
object_types: site type: port and merchant quarter;ivory santo;porcelain
leaves_out: Sangley Chinese artisans; enslaved people shipped on the galleons

name: Malacca
making_significance: Malacca was the entrepôt where Indian textiles were exchanged for spices and Chinese goods before and after Portuguese capture in 1511.

name: Banda Islands
making_significance: The only source of nutmeg and mace, Banda was conquered by the VOC in 1621 and its people killed or expelled, with plantations worked by enslaved labour.
object_types: site type: spice islands and plantations;nutmeg
leaves_out: the Bandanese and the enslaved plantation workers

name: Trowulan
making_significance: The Majapahit capital had brick temples, canals and workshops making terracotta figures and roof tiles.
object_types: site type: royal capital;terracotta figure;roof tile

name: Belitung shipwreck
making_significance: A ship of Arab or Indian build sank carrying tens of thousands of Changsha bowls and gold and silver; its commercial salvage led museums to refuse to show it.

name: Samarkand
making_significance: Samarkand was a Sogdian and later Timurid city whose murals, paper-making and tilework record Silk Road workshops.

name: Bukhara
making_significance: Bukhara's bazaars and domed trading halls served a city known for silk, gold embroidery and suzani.

name: Kashgar
making_significance: Kashgar was an oasis market where routes around the Taklamakan met, trading silk, jade and craft goods.

name: Hotan jade rivers
other_names: Yurungkash and Karakash rivers, Hotan, Xinjiang, China
making_significance: Nephrite pebbles from Hotan's rivers were carved in China for thousands of years and traded along the southern Silk Road.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);National Palace Museum Open Data (licence to verify)
notes: Hotan origin of Shang jades debated.

name: Turfan
other_names: Gaochang, Astana and Bezeklik, Xinjiang, China
making_significance: Astana tombs preserved textiles and paper reused in burial goods, and Bezeklik's murals were cut out by German expeditions in 1905.
object_types: site type: oasis city, cemetery and cave temples;textile;mural;document
free_sources: International Dunhuang Programme (link-out);collection search link-out only

name: Sar-i Sang
making_significance: Sar-i Sang is the main ancient source of lapis lazuli traded to Mesopotamia, Egypt and South Asia, and later ground for ultramarine.
leaves_out: the miners today
notes: links: NET018. Recent mining revenue linked to armed groups (to verify).

name: Gonur Depe
making_significance: A walled BMAC centre with workshops, seals and elite burials in the Murghab delta.
object_types: site type: walled centre and cemetery;seal;vessel

name: Bamiyan
making_significance: The colossal Buddhas were destroyed in 2001, and cave murals there include some of the earliest known oil-based paint.
notes: Oil paint findings: Cotte et al. 2008.

name: Tillya Tepe
making_significance: Six graves held thousands of gold ornaments mixing steppe, Greek and Indian motifs, hidden during war and shown again from 2003.

name: Karakorum
making_significance: The Mongol capital housed artisans taken from conquered cities, including the Parisian goldsmith who made a silver fountain tree.
defined_by: the Mongol court; William of Rubruck
leaves_out: the deported artisans

name: Mal'ta
making_significance: Ivory figurines, plaques and beads from Mal'ta, and the burial of a child, show Ice Age carving in Siberia.

name: Gasya
making_significance: Gasya has some of the earliest known pottery in the Russian Far East.

name: Pazyryk
making_significance: Frozen burials held felt hangings, saddles, tattooed bodies and the earliest known knotted-pile carpet.

name: Kyakhta
making_significance: Kyakhta was the border market where Chinese tea and silk were exchanged for Siberian furs.

name: Norilsk
making_significance: Nickel and copper mining at Norilsk began with Gulag prisoners and is among the world's most polluting operations.
leaves_out: the prisoners who built it; Indigenous reindeer herders

name: Uruk
making_significance: Uruk's Eanna precinct yielded early proto-cuneiform tablets, mass-produced bevelled-rim bowls and cone mosaics from one of the earliest cities in Mesopotamia.
object_types: site type: city and temple precinct;clay tablet;bevelled-rim bowl;cylinder seal
functions: record and writing;food and storage;ritual and belief
leaves_out: the workers paid in rations recorded on the tablets

name: Royal Cemetery of Ur
making_significance: Tombs at Ur held lyres, the 'Standard of Ur', gold headdresses and etched carnelian beads from the Indus, divided in 1922-34 between London, Philadelphia and Baghdad.
functions: ritual and belief;rule and display;play and music
leaves_out: the attendants killed and buried with the dead; Iraqi workmen
free_sources: British Museum collection search (link-out);collection search link-out only;Wikimedia Commons

name: Nimrud
making_significance: The Assyrian capital's palaces held carved reliefs and thousands of ivories from Levantine workshops, and were deliberately destroyed in 2015.
object_types: site type: royal capital;ivory plaque;relief;gold jewellery
leaves_out: the Levantine carvers whose ivories came as tribute and booty
free_sources: British Museum collection search (link-out);Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: Babylon
making_significance: Moulded, glazed bricks of the Ishtar Gate and Processional Way were excavated by German teams and rebuilt in Berlin.
object_types: site type: city and gate;glazed brick panel

name: Samarra
making_significance: The Abbasid palace city had lustre-painted pottery and tiles, bevelled-style stucco and imported Chinese ceramics.
object_types: site type: palace city;lustre bowl;stucco panel

name: Raqqa
making_significance: Raqqa had glass and ceramic industries from the Abbasid period to the 13th century, and its sites were heavily looted from 2011.
object_types: site type: city and industrial quarter;Raqqa-ware jar;glass

name: Madinat al-Salam
making_significance: Baghdad's paper mills from the late 8th century supplied a book trade and chancery on a new scale.
notes: links: INV037. Mill founding c. 794-95 per later sources.

name: Iraq Museum
making_significance: The national museum, founded under Gertrude Bell, lost thousands of objects in April 2003 looting, many later recovered.
leaves_out: Iraqi archaeologists who defined the collections

name: Susa
making_significance: Susa's painted pottery, Elamite works and Achaemenid glazed-brick archers were excavated under a French monopoly and largely sent to the Louvre.
leaves_out: Iranian workers; Iran's share of finds

name: Shahr-i Sokhta
making_significance: Workshops at the 'Burnt City' worked lapis, carnelian and turquoise into beads on the route from Afghanistan westward.

name: Konar Sandal
making_significance: Carved chlorite vessels from Jiroft were looted in large numbers after floods in 2001 before excavation began.
object_types: site type: mound and cemetery;chlorite vessel

name: Persepolis
making_significance: Persepolis tablets record rations for kurtas, dependent workers including named craftsmen and women, who built and decorated the palaces.
leaves_out: the kurtas, many of them deportees

name: Kashan
making_significance: Kashan potters made lustre and mina'i fritware, and Abu'l Qasim of the Abu Tahir family wrote a treatise on it in 1301.
object_types: site type: pottery centre;lustre tile;mina'i bowl
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: Siraf
making_significance: Siraf was a Gulf port of the Abbasid era, where excavations found Chinese ceramics shipped for the Middle East.

name: Hormuz
making_significance: The island kingdom controlled the Gulf entrance and its textile, horse and spice trade until Portuguese and then Safavid control.

name: Naqsh-e Jahan and Qaysariyya bazaar
making_significance: Shah Abbas's square and royal bazaar linked court workshops for carpets, textiles and tiles to merchants, including Armenian traders.
object_types: site type: royal square and bazaar;carpet;tile panel

name: Nishapur
making_significance: Nishapur potters made slip-painted wares with Arabic inscriptions, excavated by the Met in 1935-40 and divided with Iran.

name: Jericho
making_significance: Early Neolithic Jericho built a stone tower and walls and plastered and modelled faces on human skulls.

name: 'Ain Ghazal
making_significance: Lime-plaster statues on reed cores, about 9,000 years old, were buried in caches at 'Ain Ghazal.

name: Jerusalem glassblowing workshop
making_significance: Glass tubes and blown bottles from workshop debris are among the earliest evidence of glassblowing.

name: Timna
date_note: approx.; peaks in New Kingdom and 10th c. BCE
making_significance: Timna's mines and smelting camps supplied copper under Egyptian and then local control, with a Hathor shrine at the mines.

name: Faynan
other_names: Wadi Faynan and Khirbat en-Nahas, Jordan
making_significance: Faynan was copper-mined from the Chalcolithic to Roman times, when condemned Christians worked its mines.
leaves_out: condemned mine labourers under Rome
notes: Eusebius records Christians sent to the Phaino mines.

name: Ugarit
making_significance: Ugarit's archives, including a cuneiform alphabet, and its ivory and bronze workshops record a port linking Cyprus, Egypt and Anatolia.
object_types: site type: port city and palace;tablet;ivory panel

name: Tyre
making_significance: Tyre gave its name to the murex purple dye whose production left large shell middens.
object_types: site type: port city;dyed textile;shell midden
leaves_out: the dyers who handled the shells

name: Palmyra
making_significance: The caravan city's tombs held carved portraits and textiles including Chinese silk, and many monuments were destroyed in 2015.
object_types: site type: caravan city and tombs;funerary portrait;textile

name: Qal'at al-Bahrain
making_significance: The tell at Qal'at al-Bahrain was the port of Dilmun, whose round stamp seals record trade between Mesopotamia and the Indus.

name: Dilmun Burial Mounds
making_significance: Thousands of burial mounds, including royal ones at A'ali, show how Dilmun society built for its dead.

name: Maysar
making_significance: Smelting sites at Maysar produced the copper of Magan that Mesopotamian texts record being shipped to Ur.
object_types: site type: settlement and smelting site;copper ingot

name: Umm an-Nar
making_significance: Circular stone tombs at Umm an-Nar held imported pottery and beads from Mesopotamia and the Indus.
